hints: Focus on what sp hybridisation means for nitrogen, one s plus one p mixing to give two sp hybrids and leaving two p orbitals untouched.
Remember each N in N2 needs one sigma bond, two pi bonds for the triple bond, plus one lone pair, so count how the two sp orbitals and two p orbitals are used.
Think about which orbitals can overlap head-on for the sigma bond and which hybrid orbital is left over to hold the lone pair pointing away from the bond.
walkthrough:
**Start with the nitrogen atom**

Think of each N as $1s^2 2s^2 2p^3$. It has 5 valence electrons to place.

Valence configuration:
$$2s^2 2p_x^1 2p_y^1 2p_z^1$$

**Apply sp hybridisation**

One 2s and one 2p (say $2p_x$) mix to make two $sp$ hybrid orbitals. That leaves two pure p orbitals untouched.

$$1 \times 2s + 1 \times 2p \rightarrow 2 \times sp + 2 \times p \text{ (unhybridised)}$$

**Build the triple bond in N2**

The $N \equiv N$ bond is one sigma plus two pi bonds. The two pi bonds must come from sideways overlap of the two leftover p orbitals on each atom ($p_y + p_y$ and $p_z + p_z$).

**Place the sigma bond and lone pair**

That leaves the two $sp$ orbitals on each N. One $sp$ points toward the other N and overlaps head-on to make the sigma bond, so $sp$ overlaps with $sp$. The other $sp$ points away and holds the lone pair. This matches the correct row.

options.A: The sigma bond part is right, $sp$ overlaps with $sp$ head-on. But the lone pair is not in a pure p orbital. The pure p orbitals are both used for pi bonding, so the lone pair must be in the second $sp$ hybrid.
options.B: Correct. One $sp$ from each N overlaps head-on to form the sigma bond, the two unhybridised p orbitals on each N form the two pi bonds, and the remaining $sp$ on each N pointing away from the bond holds the lone pair.
options.C: Incorrect on both columns. Once hybridised, we no longer describe bonding as pure s overlapping with pure p. The sigma bond is $sp$ with $sp$. Also the lone pair is not in a pure p, as both p orbitals are used in pi bonds.
options.D: The lone pair in $sp$ is correct, but the sigma bond description is wrong. Students choosing this forget that hybridisation has occurred, so the s and p no longer exist separately for sigma bonding. It is $sp$ overlapping with $sp$.
